title.en: Where did your shirt button come from?

text.en: Look at the plastic button on your shirt. Follow its story back: oil from the ground, a factory, a shop. At some point everything around us leads back to nature.

Nature means all the living and non-living things that humans did not create, and when we use them they become resources.
For something to be a resource it must be technologically accessible, economically feasible to use, and culturally acceptable.
Cutting trees in a sacred grove may be possible but is culturally unacceptable, so such trees are not treated as a resource.
Natural resources are classified as renewable, like sunlight and wind, which can be replaced, and non-renewable, like coal and petroleum, which are used up.
They can also be biotic, from living things such as forests and fish, and abiotic, such as minerals and water.
Resources are spread unevenly across the world, so different regions depend on different resources and trade with each other.
In many indigenous traditions nature is sacred and a nurturer, as in Tulasi puja or sacred groves.
Over-exploitation, such as cutting too many forests or using too much groundwater, leads to scarcity and pollution.
Sustainable use means meeting present needs without harming the needs of future generations.
A regenerative economy repurposes used resources, minimises waste and replenishes depleted resources, following the wisdom of nature.

problem.en: Classify: coal, sunlight, fish, iron ore.

text.en: Coal and iron ore are non-renewable and abiotic.

why.en: They take millions of years to form.

text.en: Fish are renewable and biotic if not over-fished.

prompt.en: Why is a sacred tree not always a resource even though it is wood?

requiredIdeas.en: A resource must be culturally acceptable.
Cutting a sacred tree is not accepted.
So it is not used as a resource.

points.en: Nature becomes a resource when it is accessible, feasible and acceptable.
Resources are renewable or non-renewable, biotic or abiotic.
